item.title: Dad: Bring it home

item.content:encoded:
Those were the words of encouragement from Fiji Amateur Boxing Association president Panapasa Daunakamakama to his daughter Jasmine after she secured a place in the semi-finals of the women’s 57kg division at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games in Scotland.

Jasmine kept Fiji’s medal hopes alive after defeating Sri Lanka’s Keshani Hansika by a 4-1 split points decision in the quarter-finals, guaranteeing herself at least a bronze medal and moving within one win of the gold medal bout.

Speaking from his office in Wailada, Lami yesterday, Panapasa said the achievement belonged to everyone who had supported Jasmine throughout her journey.

“The glory goes back to God, and everyone involved in the journey. From the coaches to the technical team, to the family support and the support from all coaches and judges, this is for everyone,” he said.

Reflecting on Jasmine’s preparation before the Games, Panapasa said he believed she was ready for the challenge.

“Before she went into the Commonwealth Games, I knew she had ticked all the boxes which she hadn’t going into previous professional competitions.”

The proud father said he reminded Jasmine of the biblical story of David and Goliath after her quarter-final victory.

“It was a proud moment for everyone involved and when I spoke to her after the quarter final I reminded her of the David and Goliath story from the bible.

“I know it is going to get tough from here but my message to her was to ‘Bring it home.”

Jasmine will step back into the ring at 6am tomorrow, with victory in the semi-final earning her a place in the gold medal bout as she continues her pursuit of Commonwealth Games glory.

item.title: Jasmine inspires a new generation
item.description: JASMINE Daunakamakama has already guaranteed herself a place in Fiji’s sporting history. Now, professional boxer Winston Hill believes her Commonwealth Games breakthrough could transform women’s boxing in the country for years to come.
item.content:encoded:
JASMINE Daunakamakama has already guaranteed herself a place in Fiji’s sporting history.

Now, professional boxer Winston Hill believes her Commonwealth Games breakthrough could transform women’s boxing in the country for years to come.

The former Commonwealth Games bronze medallist says Daunakamakama’s march into the women’s 57kg semi-finals in Glasgow is a milestone that extends far beyond the ring.

“There is just so much pride around not just Jasmine but the whole Fijian team,” Hill said.

“History has been made with Jasmine. She is the first Fijian female boxer to reach this stage at the Commonwealth Games, and she has already secured a bronze medal.”

Daunakamakama now faces the toughest test of her career against reigning 2022 Commonwealth Games gold medalist Northern Ireland’s Michaela Walsh for a place in the gold medal bout.

Hill knows exactly what it takes to compete on boxing’s biggest amateur stage. He claimed bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast and said the occasion demands as much mental strength as physical preparation.

“When I competed in the amateurs, it was my closest moment with God,” he said.

“I went through a very strong spiritual journey during training and out on the field of play. I’m sure with her people behind her, her country and her faith, she will make Fiji proud no matter what happens.”

Hill said there was no need for Daunakamakama to change her approach despite the magnitude of the contest.

“This is her first international competition, and she has already reached the semi-finals. That is a huge milestone. She should take everything in, enjoy the experience and keep building from here.”

“The national coach is doing a fantastic job preparing both the men and Jasmine. She just needs to give it her best and know the whole country is proud of her.”

A victory over Walsh would secure at least a silver medal and put Daunakamakama within one win of Commonwealth Games gold.

For Hill, that achievement would deserve recognition far beyond the boxing community.

“If she beats Michaela Walsh, she goes into the gold or silver fight. That would be amazing,” he said.

“She deserves to come back to Fiji and be recognised. Businesses and corporate sponsors should get behind her and help create a solid pathway for her future.

“It is not just about Jasmine. It is about inspiring more young women to take up boxing.”

The Women’s 57 kg division is one of the most fiercely competitive and star-studded brackets in the 2026 Glasgow meet with nine countries represented in the division.

While it has a modest field size, the concentration of elite, world-class talent makes it a major highlight of the Games.

Away from boxing, Daunakamakama has also pursued her passion for music.

She was part of the V5 band that reached the top 10 of the national Domo Vou Talei songwriting competition with their original song Mango Tree, highlighting the talent and determination that have now carried her onto the Commonwealth Games podium.

Hill believes Daunakamakama’s historic campaign has shown that Fijian women can compete with the world’s best and could become the spark that lifts women’s boxing to new heights in Fiji.

Jasmine Daunakamakama’s semifinal bout is set for tomorrow morning, Saturday August 1, 2026, at 6am.

item.title: Suva netters rally on
item.description: SUVA Sangam College open grade team is determined to build on its Suva Zone Two success when it competes at the Central Rally this week. Open grade captain Fipe Sorocala, a year thirteen student, said the team had put in the hard work during the lead-up to the tournament and was confident of taking on the top schools.
item.content:encoded:
SUVA Sangam College open grade team is determined to build on its Suva Zone Two success when it competes at the Central Rally this week.

Open grade captain Fipe Sorocala, a year thirteen student, said the team had put in the hard work during the lead-up to the tournament and was confident of taking on the top schools.

“We have been preparing throughout the week,” Sorocala said.

The team heads into the competition after claiming the Suva Zone Two title, a result that has boosted the players’ confidence ahead of the Central Rally.

Fipe acknowledged that the standard of competition would be much higher but said the players were looking forward to the challenge.

“We are excited, and we are prepared to face the bigger schools,” she said.

Sorocala said the team had focused on building strong combinations and improving communication during training, which had helped strengthen the players’ understanding of one another.

“We have prepared ourselves well over the past few days, and everyone knows their role within the team.

We are ready to move forward,” she said.

Sorocala believes the team’s preparation and unity will be key as Suva Sangam aims to continue its winning form and challenge for top honours at the Central Rally.

item.title: Singh wants strong finish
item.description: NAVUA will look to turn its recent lessons into a stronger performance when it meets a determined Tailevu Naitasiri side in the Extra Premier League Round 16 clash on Sunday. Coach Rodicks Singh expects a demanding contest, with Tailevu Naitasiri fighting to keep its place in the competition and likely to bring plenty of intensity to the match.
item.content:encoded:
NAVUA will look to turn its recent lessons into a stronger performance when it meets a determined Tailevu Naitasiri side in the Extra Premier League Round 16 clash on Sunday.

Coach Rodicks Singh expects a demanding contest, with Tailevu Naitasiri fighting to keep its place in the competition and likely to bring plenty of intensity to the match.

“The preparations and expectations are both going to need to be very intense because we know we’re playing a side that is fighting for survival,” Singh said.

For Navua, the match presents an opportunity to build on its strengths while addressing areas that have prevented the team from producing consistent performances.

Singh believes his players have shown what they are capable of but wants them to find greater consistency from one match to the next.

“We’re not consistent. We win one week; we have come down with two losses back-to-back. We are not consistent in the way we want to play,” he said.

The coach said the focus now is on turning those lessons into improvement and ensuring the team maintains its intensity throughout the match.

Finishing strongly is another area Navua is working to improve.

“Our finishing part is still a very worrying factor. Our area of concern is how we finish the game,” Singh said.

He said the team has allowed its intensity to drop during the final 15 minutes of recent matches, giving opponents opportunities to take advantage.

“If you look at the past two games, it is the last part of the game that is really hurting us,” he said.

item.title: Skipper Cup first round kick starts tomorrow
item.description: THE race for the 2026 Skipper Cup competition intensifies this weekend as Fiji’s top 12 provincial teams battle it off in round one of the competition. Defending champions Malolo will be aiming to retain the crown after an impressive debut campaign last year, but they are expected to face stiff competition from a strong field eager to make an early statement.
item.content:encoded:
THE race for the 2026 Skipper Cup competition intensifies this weekend as Fiji’s top 12 provincial teams battle it off in round one of the competition.

Defending champions Malolo will be aiming to retain the crown after an impressive debut campaign last year, but they are expected to face stiff competition from a strong field eager to make an early statement.

Adding excitement to the competition are newcomers Rewa and Taveuni, who earned their Skipper Cup promotion earlier this year.

Taveuni will be making their debut while Rewa is making an appearance after an absence of three years from the competition.

Both sides will be looking to prove whether they belong among Fiji’s elite provisional teams and make a positive start to their campaigns.

With the competition kicking off for round one, every team will be looking to build momentum, knowing each result could prove crucial later in the season.

Round one kicks of this Saturday, August 1; Malolo v Taveuni at Lawaqa Park, Rewa v Naitasiri at Burebasaga grounds, Navosa v Tailevu Vatureba park, Keasi, Nadi v Kadavu at King Charles Park, Suva v Ba at HFC Bank stadium, Lautoka v Nadroga Churchill park.

item.title: Big plans for games in Ba
item.description: INTERNATIONAL night games could soon be coming to Govind Park as the Ba Town Council moves to equip the 4R Stadium with high-powered floodlights required to host world-class evening tournaments. Special Administrators board chairman Moshim Khan confirmed that installing permanent lighting capable of delivering a minimum of 1,500 lux is the council’s top operational objective for the venue.
item.content:encoded:
INTERNATIONAL night games could soon be coming to Govind Park as the Ba Town Council moves to equip the 4R Stadium with high-powered floodlights required to host world-class evening tournaments.

Special Administrators board chairman Moshim Khan confirmed that installing permanent lighting capable of delivering a minimum of 1,500 lux is the council’s top operational objective for the venue.

“At this moment our main priority is to get the permanent floodlight, which meets the 1,500 lux so that we can have international night games,” he said.

While the stadium successfully hosted 14,000 spectators during last year’s Inter-District Championship, Mr Khan said substantial work remains before the facility can consistently attract global events after dark.

“We are trying to improve day by day to give a better facility.

“There is a lot of work left to do to actually meet the requirements of international tournaments.”

To support this shift toward international-grade hosting, the council is planning broader infrastructure additions, including corporate boxes and possibly a potential expansion on the opposite side of the grounds however this is still in the discussion stage.

“It’s not only about the staff and the stadium, everything has to be of international standard.

“Even the food they’re selling has to be compliant with the Food and Safety Act.”

item.title: Boost for Rewa ahead of OCL
item.description: Rewa FC has received a timely boost ahead of its OFC Men’s Champions League 2026 campaign after the Fiji Football Association presented the Delta Tigers with financial assistance as they prepare to represent the country on home soil. The sponsorship cheque was presented yesterday at the Fiji FA Academy in Vatuwaqa, where Rewa is completing its final preparations for the regional championship, whic
item.content:encoded:
Rewa FC has received a timely boost ahead of its OFC Men’s Champions League 2026 campaign after the Fiji Football Association presented the Delta Tigers with financial assistance as they prepare to represent the country on home soil.

The sponsorship cheque was presented yesterday at the Fiji FA Academy in Vatuwaqa, where Rewa is completing its final preparations for the regional championship, which will be held in Fiji from August 9-22.

The Delta Tigers qualified for the competition after winning the 2025 Extra Premier League title and will be making their third consecutive appearance in Oceania’s premier club tournament.

FFA president Rajesh Patel said supporting Rewa was part of Fiji FA’s commitment to ensuring the nation’s representative had every opportunity to succeed.

“It is costing us a lot of money to host the championship in Fiji, but we believe it is an investment in the development of football and in giving our representative club the best possible opportunity to compete,” Patel said.

“Playing at home provides Rewa with a great chance to challenge for the title, and we hope they make the most of this opportunity.”

Rewa FC senior vice-president Sanjay Patel thanked Fiji FA for both the financial contribution and access to the Fiji FA Academy.

“We sincerely thank Fiji FA for its generous support. The financial assistance, together with the use of the Fiji FA Academy for our training camp, has been invaluable to our preparations,” Patel said.

“We are proud to represent Fiji on the regional stage. Winning the OFC Champions League would be the biggest achievement in the history of our club, and the players and officials are committed to giving their very best.”

Patel also highlighted the club’s Red Kaji Kaji grassroots program, which currently involves 218 children aged six to 14, reflecting Rewa’s commitment to developing future football talent while pursuing regional success.

item.title: Potter back with Bati
item.description: MICK Potter has returned with unfinished business. The coach who guided the Fiji Bati to a historic Rugby League World Cup semi-final in 2017 is back at the helm.
item.content:encoded:
MICK Potter has returned with unfinished business.

The coach who guided the Fiji Bati to a historic Rugby League World Cup semi-final in 2017 is back at the helm.

This time, he wants more than another successful campaign. He wants to transform rugby league in Fiji from the ground up.

Potter made his first public comments yesterday at the as the new Fiji Bati head coach after being endorsed by the Fiji National Rugby League board following an open recruitment process.

The veteran Australian said returning to Fiji was both an honour and an emotional moment.

“I’m honoured to be in this position. I’m grateful for the board of the Fiji National Rugby League to appoint me,” Potter said.

“It’s a thing that I’m pretty passionate about and I’m emotional about.”

While the countdown to the Rugby League World Cup has already begun, Potter said Fiji’s long-term future would be built away from the international spotlight.

He intends to spend time in communities, schools and clubs to strengthen the game’s foundations.

“I feel that Fiji Rugby League, in the last 10 years, we need to move forward,” he said.

“I think we’ve just stayed flat, and I really want to make a statement that I’m going to get out into the fields, get out into the community, into the schools, into the clubs, and really push rugby league.”

Potter believes Fiji has the talent to become one of the world’s elite rugby league nations.

“We want to be a Tier One nation in rugby league,” he said.

“We want to be one of the top four nations and I think we can do it.”

He admitted the journey would take time but said the goal was achievable with the right people driving the game.

Potter also acknowledged the volunteers and administrators who continue to keep the game alive across the country.

“There are so many lovely people out there that want to help rugby league and I’m very grateful to them and I can’t wait to get out there and work with them.”

FNRL executive chairman Rajesh Singh said Potter’s appointment followed a competitive selection process after the previous coach’s contract expired.

He backed Potter to recreate the success of his first stint, when Fiji recorded its famous victory over New Zealand before reaching the 2017 Rugby League World Cup semi-finals.

With just 77 days remaining before the Rugby League World Cup, Potter’s second chapter with the Fiji Bati has officially begun—this time with his sights set on building a legacy that extends well beyond the tournament.
